question: Does Pleasant Park have lights?
answer: No, and it is a verified no rather than a gap. The town's court table reads "No" in the Lights column, and the park's own page gives basketball and pickleball court hours as sunrise to thirty minutes after sunset. It is the only unlit pickleball site in Apex, and also the largest.

question: Can I check if the courts are busy before I go?
answer: Yes, uniquely. Pleasant Park's page carries a live court occupancy feed for its pickleball courts. No other venue in this directory publishes real-time availability.

question: How many courts are there?
answer: Six, and the town says so twice: its court table lists Pleasant Park with 6, and the park's own features list reads "6 Pickleball courts". That makes it the biggest verified pickleball site in Apex.

question: Are the courts at Kelly Road Park dedicated to pickleball?
answer: No. The park's own features list calls them "4 junior tennis / pickleball courts", and the town's table notes they are also used for junior tennis. You will be playing on a junior tennis surface with pickleball lines on it.

question: Can I play here in the evening?
answer: The town marks this venue as lit and publishes park hours of 6:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. year round. It does not state what time the lights come on or whether they are switched or timed.

question: Is there a restroom?
answer: Yes, restroom facilities are listed among the park's features on its own page.

question: Is Kelly Road Park the same as “Apex Kelly Rd Park”?
answer: Yes. The commercial dataset this directory started from holds two separate rows for this one park — “Kelly Road Park” and “Apex Kelly Rd Park” — both claiming four courts at the same place. We publish one venue, matched to the town's own record, and leave the duplicate row unpublished. Two rows for one park is an identity problem in the source data, and the fix is to resolve it rather than to quietly pick one and hope nobody notices the other.

question: Which entrance do I want for the pickleball courts?
answer: 2500 Evans Road, the Seymour Athletic Fields entrance. The other entrance, at 2600 Evans Road, opens onto the nature park side with the dog park, disc golf and amphitheatre. The town says there are parking lots at both and a paved walkway connecting them.

question: How many pickleball courts are there?
answer: Four, from the town's court table, which also notes they are used for junior tennis. The park's own page confirms the courts exist and are lit but does not give a number, so this is the one Apex count that rests on a single page rather than two.

question: What is this venue actually called?
answer: The town uses two names. Its pickleball table says "Seymour Athletic Fields at Apex Nature Park"; the park page heads the section "Seymour Athletic fields" within a page titled Apex Nature Park & Seymour Athletic Fields. We publish the shorter form because the full one overruns the page-title limit.

question: How many pickleball courts does Apex Community Park have?
answer: Three, and they are lit. The park's own features list states "3 lighted pickleball courts" outright, and the town's court table gives the same figure with Lights marked Yes.

question: Which entrance should I use?
answer: The park entrance at 2200 Laura Duncan Road. The park publishes a second entrance, the Lake Trail entrance at 1808 Lake Pine Drive, which serves the lake and trails rather than the courts.

question: What else is at this park?
answer: A great deal: six tennis courts, two basketball courts, three sand volleyball courts, two street hockey rinks, three ball fields with batting cages reserved for league play, a fitness course, playgrounds, restrooms, over three miles of trails, and a 50-plus acre lake with an accessible fishing dock and a vessel launch.

question: Who can play indoors here?
answer: Players aged 55 and over, during designated open gym hours. That restriction comes from the town's own court table, and it publishes a separate Senior 55+ Indoor Pickleball Calendar for the schedule.

question: Why are there no opening hours listed for this venue?
answer: Because the town publishes the building's hours, not the courts'. Pickleball runs during designated open gym hours, which is a subset of the time the building is open, so listing the building's hours as court hours would tell you that you can play at times when you cannot. We leave it unverified and point you at the calendar.

question: Is this the same place as the Apex Community Center?
answer: Yes. The town states that the John M. Brown Community Center was formerly known as the Apex Community Center. That statement is what tied the old record in our imported data to the current facility, and both give the same count of four courts.

question: Are these really the only verified indoor courts on this site?
answer: Yes, at the time of writing. Every other venue in this directory is outdoors. Raleigh runs indoor open play at thirteen community centres and Cary rents three indoor courts at Middle Creek, but neither publishes what we need — Raleigh gives no per-centre court count and Cary gives no street address — so neither publishes as a venue.

question: Can I reserve a pickleball court at McCrimmon?
answer: No. The town marks the pickleball courts "Non-reservable, first-come, first-served". The lighted tennis court at the same park is reservable sixteen hours in advance, which is the opposite of what most people expect.

question: How many pickleball courts are there?
answer: Six. The park's own page confirms lighted pickleball courts without giving a number; the count comes from the Cary Tennis Park page, which lists this site as having "Six Lighted Tennis Courts and Six Lighted Pickleball Courts".

question: Can I play here in the evening?
answer: The courts are lit, and Cary runs open play here on Monday evenings from 7 to 9 p.m. Park hours are sunrise to sunset with an extension only for approved extended-use activities, up to 11 p.m. at the latest, so lighting does not by itself guarantee late casual play.

question: Is this the same place as McCrimmon Park?
answer: Yes. The town's own park page calls it the Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway; its Cary Tennis Park page calls it McCrimmon Park. We publish the park's own name and treat the shorter one as an alias.

question: Does Ed Yerha Park have lights?
answer: The town does not say, so we do not claim it either way. Its page states no lighting for the courts and gives park hours as sunrise to sunset with no extension clause, unlike two other Cary parks. Treat it as a daylight venue until the town says otherwise.

question: Is this the same as White Oak Park?
answer: Yes. Ed Yerha Park is the former White Oak Park, renamed for a councilmember who served from 2012 to 2022. The town's own page explains the change, and its open data still carries the old name on the same map point.

question: Do I need to book a court?
answer: No. The town's status board for the park reads "Pickleball Courts Open - First Come, First Served". The picnic shelter is reservable; the courts are not.

question: Are the pickleball courts at Carpenter Park dedicated?
answer: No. The town lists them as "Multi-Sport Courts: Basketball & 3 Pickleball Courts", so the three pickleball courts share their surface with basketball and you will be playing over other lines.

question: Is there parking at Carpenter Park?
answer: Yes, and unusually the town says how much: "Parking for 30 Cars". No time limit, permit or fee is published. Bear in mind those thirty spaces serve a 16-acre park with a playground, community garden, picnic shelter, trails and a memorial as well as the courts.

question: Can I play here after dark?
answer: Not on anything the town has published. Park hours are sunrise to sunset, with an extension only in lighted areas for approved extended-use activities. The page does not state that the pickleball courts themselves are lit, so we record lighting as not verified. Of Cary's three verified parks, only the Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway has lighted pickleball courts stated outright.

question: How many pickleball courts does Clarks Creek Park have?
answer: Eight. Mecklenburg County names them individually rather than giving a total: courts 1 to 5 are reservable and courts 6 to 8 are open play, which is a complete run from 1 to 8 with no gaps and no court listed twice.

question: Can I play here without booking?
answer: Yes, on three of the eight. Courts 6, 7 and 8 are permanently open play and cannot be reserved. That is the largest guaranteed walk-up allocation at any Charlotte park in this set.

question: Are the courts lit?
answer: We do not know. Mecklenburg County publishes no lighting information for any of its courts, so this reads "Not verified yet" rather than yes or no. It is an absence of published information, not evidence that the courts are unlit.

question: Is this the same as Clarks Creek Nature Preserve?
answer: No. The city's parks layer holds them as separate records on opposite sides of Hucks Road — the park at 5435 and the nature preserve at 5434 — and there is a third record, Clarks Creek Greenway Park, on Mallard Creek Road. The pickleball is at 5435 Hucks Road.

question: Why do Freedom Park's pickleball courts start at number 11?
answer: Because courts 1 to 10 at the same park are tennis courts, listed separately on the county's page. Mecklenburg runs one numbering series across both sports at this site instead of restarting it, so the pickleball block begins where the tennis block ends.

question: How many pickleball courts are there, and which can I book?
answer: Six, numbered 11 to 16. Courts 11, 12, 14 and 15 are reservable for a small fee; courts 13 and 16 are permanently open play. The county does not publish what the fee is.

question: Are the courts lit?
answer: Unknown. Mecklenburg County publishes no lighting information for any court in its system, so this reads "Not verified yet". Raleigh and Apex both publish lighting for every location; Charlotte does not.

question: How many courts are there and which are bookable?
answer: Six, numbered 1 to 6. Courts 1 to 4 are reservable for a small fee the county does not price; courts 5 and 6 are permanently open play and cannot be reserved.

question: Which postcode is right, 28217 or 28208?
answer: 28217, on the evidence we have. The City of Charlotte parks layer gives 28217 for 1520 Clanton Road; the commercial dataset we started from carries 28208 for its Clanton Park row. We publish the operator's figure and record the disagreement rather than averaging two numbers that cannot both be right.

question: Is this the same as Clanton Park Community Garden?
answer: No. The city's parks layer holds the community garden as a separate record at a different address on Revolution Park Drive. The pickleball courts are at 1520 Clanton Road.

question: How does the county decide which courts are bookable?
answer: It does not say, and the pattern is only visible once you line the parks up. Mecklenburg reserves most courts and keeps some back at every single one of its five pickleball parks — three at Clarks Creek, two here, two at Freedom, two at Martin Luther King Jr. and one at Beatty. Nineteen of the county's 29 courts are reservable and ten are permanently open play. So the policy is consistent even though it is never stated as a policy: whatever else is booked, a walk-up player always has somewhere to go, though at Beatty that means a single court.

question: Which courts can I use without booking?
answer: Courts 1 and 4. Mecklenburg County lists courts 2, 3, 5 and 6 as reservable and leaves 1 and 4 as open play, so those two are always available first come, first served.

question: Is this the same as Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School?
answer: No. The city's parks layer holds the middle school as a separate record on Bilmark Avenue. The park with the pickleball courts is at 2600 Ravencroft Drive.

question: What does the county publish about the courts themselves?
answer: Almost nothing. It identifies six courts and tells you which four are bookable. It publishes no lighting, no surface, no nets information, no hours and no reservation price for this or any other park in its system.

question: How does this park compare with the rest of Charlotte?
answer: It sits in the middle. Six courts puts it level with Clanton Park and Freedom Park, behind Clarks Creek Park's eight and ahead of Colonel Francis J. Beatty Park's three. Its two guaranteed walk-up courts are the same allocation Clanton and Freedom get. What is unusual here is only the arrangement: at the other parks the open-play courts sit together at one end of the run, while here they are courts 1 and 4, spaced through the six.

question: Does the county publish opening hours?
answer: Not for this park or any other. It says only that its local park courts "are always open for play", which describes access rather than a timetable — it does not tell you when the park gates close. We record hours as not verified rather than reading that sentence as round-the-clock access, which it plainly is not meant to be.

question: Is this park in Charlotte or Matthews?
answer: Charlotte, though it takes a third source to settle it. The postcode 28105 is a Matthews mailing ZIP and many listings place the park there, while the City of Charlotte parks layer labels its city as Charlotte. The US Census geocoder places the park's published coordinates inside the incorporated place of Charlotte, in Mecklenburg County.

question: How many pickleball courts are there?
answer: Three, numbered 1 to 3. Courts 2 and 3 are reservable for a small fee; court 1 is permanently open play. The park's tennis courts continue the same numbering at 4 to 6.

question: What are my chances of getting a court without booking?
answer: Lower than anywhere else in Charlotte. Only court 1 is guaranteed open play, so if both bookable courts are reserved there is one court for every walk-up. Clarks Creek Park keeps three courts back and is the better bet if you have not booked.

question: Are the pickleball courts at Baileywick Park covered?
answer: Partly. The park page lists Court A as covered and Court B as covered centre, and pickleball is scheduled on Courts A and B, so yes — though we still count these as outdoor courts, because a roof is not the same as being indoors. Court C, which pickleball does not normally use, is uncovered.

question: When can I play pickleball at Baileywick?
answer: Raleigh Parks publishes the windows: Monday to Friday noon to 4 p.m., Saturday 3 to 9 p.m., and Sunday 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Outside those hours the same courts are scheduled for basketball open play, a youth basketball league or futsal. The park page also asks you to check its holiday schedule.

question: Is Baileywick Park open right now?
answer: Court A was closed for repairs as of 24 August 2026 and Raleigh Parks published no reopening date. Since pickleball at this park runs on Courts A and B, that is half the pickleball surface. The rest of the park was not reported closed. Check the park's page before travelling.

question: Does Baileywick Park have six pickleball courts or four?
answer: The city's two records disagree, and we would rather show you that than pick quietly. Raleigh Parks' pickleball page says six; its GIS court inventory holds polygons for Court A and Court B totalling four, and has no polygon for Court C. We publish six and have flagged the venue for a re-check.

question: Do I need to bring a net to Carolina Pines Park?
answer: Yes. Raleigh Parks' note for this location says you need to bring or borrow a net. It is one of only two Raleigh locations where the department says so outright — the other is Southgate Park.

question: Are the courts at Carolina Pines dedicated to pickleball?
answer: No. Raleigh Parks describes them as tennis courts with pickleball lines. The park's own page records three tennis courts at this site, with no backboards and push-button lighting from dusk to 10 p.m.

question: How many pickleball courts does Carolina Pines have?
answer: Raleigh Parks says four and its GIS court inventory says three. We publish the department's four, because that page states a citywide total of 44 courts which its own per-location figures add up to, and we have flagged this venue for a re-check.

question: Does Fred Fletcher Park have lights?
answer: No, and that is a verified no rather than a gap. Raleigh Parks marks the location as unlit in its pickleball table, and the park's own page records its tennis courts as having no lights. It is one of two daylight-only pickleball locations in the city.

question: What is the address of Fred Fletcher Park?
answer: The park's own page gives two frontages, 820 Clay Street and 805 Washington Street, Raleigh 27605, with entrances off St. Mary's Street and Glenwood Avenue. Ignore the "514 Method Road" that appears against this park in the city's pickleball table — that is Method Community Park's address, duplicated from the row below.

question: Are the pickleball courts here dedicated?
answer: No. Raleigh Parks describes them as tennis courts with pickleball lines. The park page records two tennis courts with no backboard, which is the surface those lines are on.

question: Can I play at Jaycee Park in the evening?
answer: Raleigh Parks marks this location as lit, and says its outdoor court lighting runs on a timer until 10 p.m. Nothing published states what time the lights come on beyond dusk, or whether the timer changes with the season.

question: Are the courts at Jaycee Park pickleball-only?
answer: No. The department lists them as tennis courts with pickleball lines, so tennis players may have them when you arrive and you will be playing over tennis lines.

question: Is there parking at Jaycee Park?
answer: The park page mentions a parking lot on Wade Avenue and says ample parking is provided on both sides of the dog run, but it is describing access to the dog run rather than to the courts. No capacity, time limit or fee is published.

question: Can I reserve a court at Method Community Park?
answer: No. Raleigh Parks marks this location "Drop in only, no reservations". Other Raleigh locations do take bookings through the department's pickleball court reservation form, but this is not one of them.

question: How late are the lights on at Method?
answer: The park's own page says the lighting is on a timer from dusk to 10 p.m., which matches the department's statement that its outdoor courts run on a lighting timer to 10 p.m.

question: Is there indoor pickleball at Method Road?
answer: The community centre on this site is one of thirteen running Raleigh's indoor open-play programme, at $3 a session or $15 for a four-month pass, with nets and balls provided. The city does not publish how many courts the gym holds for open play, so we have not verified it as a venue. The gym rental listing mentions three pickle courts and one volleyball court at $85 an hour.

question: Are Method's six courts real pickleball courts?
answer: Yes — Raleigh Parks describes them as permanent courts, and the park page lists six with backboards. Both the department's pickleball page and its GIS court inventory give the same figure of six, which is not the case at every Raleigh location.

question: Are North Hills Park's pickleball courts open?
answer: Daytime play reopened on 2 September 2026 after a lighting upgrade that began on 24 August. Night play was still closed when we checked on 3 September, with Raleigh Parks targeting 8 September for completion. Check the park's page before an evening visit.

question: Can I book a court at North Hills Park?
answer: No. Raleigh Parks marks the location "Drop in only, no reservations", and the park's own page states that court reservations are not offered during open play.

question: How many courts are there, and do the sources agree?
answer: Six, and unusually for this set every record we have says the same: the department's pickleball page, its GIS court inventory and the commercial dataset we started from all give six. Two other Raleigh venues do not have that luxury.

question: Are there lights at Powell Drive Park?
answer: Yes. Raleigh Parks marks the location as lit in its pickleball table and its GIS court inventory records lighting on the pickleball courts here. The city's outdoor court lights run on a timer until 10 p.m.

question: Do I need to bring a net to Powell Drive Park?
answer: The city does not say, either way. It tells you to bring a net at Carolina Pines and Southgate and says nothing about nets at the other nine locations, so we record nets here as not verified rather than guessing. Bringing one is the safe assumption.

question: Is there a restroom at Powell Drive Park?
answer: None is recorded in the city's park amenities inventory for this park. That inventory does record restrooms at five of the eleven Raleigh pickleball locations, so its silence here is meaningful, though we publish it as unverified rather than as a confirmed absence.

question: Is there a restroom at Roberts Park?
answer: Yes. The city's park amenities inventory records a restroom here, which is true at only five of the eleven Raleigh pickleball locations.

question: Are Roberts Park's pickleball courts dedicated?
answer: No. Raleigh Parks lists them as tennis courts with pickleball lines, so you are sharing the surface with tennis and playing over tennis markings.

question: Does it cost anything to play at Roberts Park?
answer: No fee is published for the outdoor courts, and no source states that they are free either, so we record cost as not verified. The prices Raleigh Parks does publish — $3 a session, $15 for four months — are for indoor open play at its community centres.

question: How does getting a game work here?
answer: By the city's sign-up rules, which apply at every Raleigh facility. Players sign in or place a paddle in a quadrant of four, games are singles or doubles to 11 points and win by 2, and at the end of each game all four players leave the court so the next four on the list can play. Groups who want to stay together are asked to skip to the next fully open quadrant rather than break an existing one up. With two courts at a central park, that queue is the thing most likely to decide how long you wait.

question: How many pickleball courts does Sanderford Road Park have?
answer: Ten, and it is the largest pickleball site in Raleigh. The department's pickleball page and its GIS court inventory both give ten, and they are permanent pickleball courts rather than lines on a tennis surface.

question: Can I reserve a court at Sanderford Road Park?
answer: The park's own page says court reservations are available here, and Raleigh Parks publishes a pickleball court reservation form. That is different from Method Community Park and North Hills Park, which are marked drop-in only. Check the department's monthly pickleball calendar before you travel.

question: Is there a restroom at Sanderford Road Park?
answer: None is recorded for this park in the city's park amenities inventory. We publish that as unverified rather than as a confirmed absence, but plan for it at a ten-court site where you may be there a while.

question: What is the correct address for Sanderford Road Park?
answer: 2623 Sanderford Road, Raleigh 27610. Both Raleigh Parks' pickleball page and its park amenities inventory give that number. Some third-party listings show 2823 Sanderford Road; that does not match either city record.

question: Do I need to bring a net to Southgate Park?
answer: Yes. Raleigh Parks' note for this location says you need to bring your own net. It is one of only two Raleigh locations where the department says so, the other being Carolina Pines Park.

question: Are there lights at Southgate Park?
answer: No. Raleigh Parks marks this location No in the Lights column of its pickleball table. It is one of two unlit pickleball locations in the city, with Fred Fletcher Park, so play here is limited to daylight.

question: What surface are the courts at Southgate Park?
answer: Asphalt, according to the city's GIS court inventory. Southgate is the only one of the eleven Raleigh locations where that field is filled in — everywhere else it is empty, which is why every other Raleigh venue here shows its surface as not verified.

question: Is Tarboro Road Park a good central option?
answer: It is one of the closest verified pickleball locations to downtown Raleigh, and it is lit, so it works after work. It has only two courts and they are shared with tennis, so it is a convenient option rather than a spacious one.

question: What are the opening hours for the courts?
answer: The city does not publish them. The park's page carries hours for the park, for the community centre and for the Saint Monica Teen Center, none of which is a statement about when the outdoor courts are available, so we leave court hours unverified rather than repeating a centre's opening times as if they were the courts'.

question: How many pickleball courts are at Tarboro Road Park?
answer: Two, and every record we have agrees — Raleigh Parks' pickleball page, its GIS court inventory, and the commercial dataset this directory started from. They are pickleball lines on the park's tennis courts rather than dedicated courts.

question: Can I turn up alone and get a game?
answer: Yes, during the open-play windows, and this is the only Seattle venue where that is a designed feature rather than luck. Ambassadors run a paddle stacking system in those sessions so single players rotate in. Outside those hours you are on your own like anywhere else.

question: Are these courts indoor?
answer: No. All eight are outdoor, and there is no covered or climate-controlled pickleball recorded anywhere in Seattle. An earlier commercial record claimed two indoor courts here; the city's own data does not, and we have removed the claim.

question: Is there a fee?
answer: Not verified. Seattle Parks publishes no fee information for its pickleball courts, so we show cost as unverified here as everywhere else on this site rather than assuming it is free.

question: What time do the courts close?
answer: 10 p.m. every day, with opening at 7 a.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays. These hours took effect on 15 September 2025.

question: Why does this park have hours when most do not?
answer: Noise studies run by Seattle Parks with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found play here producing sound levels above the limits in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. Gilman is one of three Seattle sites given posted hours as a result.

question: What happens if people play after 10 p.m.?
answer: The city fits a lock. A violation documented outside posted hours with timestamped visual evidence results in a temporary lock for at least thirty days; repeat violations lead to a permanent lock, after which the courts open only when staff are on site to unlock them.

question: Are nets provided?
answer: Yes. Seattle Parks records nets at this location, which is not universal — the city records nets at seventeen of its twenty-five pickleball sites and says nothing either way about the other eight, so a portable net is worth carrying if you also play elsewhere in the city.

question: Is this a dedicated pickleball court?
answer: Yes, and that is rare here. Seattle Parks records only four dedicated pickleball locations in the city and three of them, including this one, have a single court. Every other verified Seattle venue shares its surface with tennis, basketball or badminton.

question: Only one court — will I get on?
answer: That depends entirely on who else turns up, and we have no crowding data for any Seattle venue so we will not guess. One court means one game at a time and an informal rotation with whoever is waiting.

question: What time does it close?
answer: 10 p.m., opening 7 a.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays, in force since 15 September 2025 after noise studies found levels above Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08.

question: Are nets provided, and is there a restroom?
answer: Nets yes, and an all-year restroom is recorded on site, which matters more than it sounds — eleven of the twenty-five Seattle pickleball locations have only a seasonal restroom and three have none recorded at all. Dedicated parking is also recorded here rather than street parking.

question: It has lights — can I play late?
answer: Until 10 p.m. and no later. This is the only Seattle venue that is both lit and curfewed, so the lights are genuinely useful in winter afternoons and genuinely capped at night. For lit courts without a posted curfew, Bitter Lake Playfield and Rainier Beach Playfield carry no such order in the records we have checked.

question: Why is there a curfew at a lit park?
answer: The two are unrelated. The lighting is recorded by Seattle Parks as a facility; the hours were imposed in September 2025 after noise studies with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found play exceeding Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08.

question: Where do I park?
answer: Street parking — Seattle Parks records no dedicated lot here. No permit or time-limit information is published and we have not checked restrictions on the ground, so read the posted signs.

question: Is this the same place as Bitter Lake Community Center?
answer: No, and keeping them apart mattered. The community centre is a building with three indoor courts of its own; this record is the outdoor playfield with eight. They share a campus. Our imported data blurred the two into a single eleven-court entry, which the city records do not support.

question: Can I play here in the evening?
answer: The city records lighting here, and no restricted-hours order applies to this site in the records we have checked. What Seattle Parks does not publish is when the lights actually run or whether they are switched on seasonally, so treat evening play as possible rather than guaranteed.

question: Are the courts dedicated to pickleball?
answer: No. This is a shared tennis and pickleball surface, which is the norm in Seattle. Only four of the twenty-five locations the city records are dedicated pickleball, and three of those are single courts.

question: How does it compare with Rainier Beach?
answer: They are the two eight-court lit sites in Seattle and between them hold sixteen of the city's ninety-two verified courts. Rainier Beach has an all-year restroom where Bitter Lake's is seasonal; both have dedicated parking and nets. On the city's record the two are close to interchangeable, and the deciding factor for most people will be which end of Seattle they are starting from.

question: Is this the community centre?
answer: No. Seattle Parks records the playfield and the community centre separately, and this page is the playfield: eight outdoor courts. The community centre entry in our import claims three indoor courts and has not been verified, so it does not appear on this site at all.

question: Did anything change from the original data?
answer: Almost nothing, which is unusual here. The court count and the outdoor split both matched the city record exactly. The address was corrected, and everything the city does not state, including surface, fees and hours, was cleared to unverified.

question: Are there lights and a restroom?
answer: Both are recorded by the city: lighting present, and an all-year restroom rather than a seasonal one. What is not recorded anywhere is the hours those lights operate.

question: How does it compare with Bitter Lake?
answer: They are the only two eight-court lit venues in the city and are near-identical on the record: nets, dedicated parking, lights, tennis-shared. The one difference Seattle Parks records is the restroom, all-year here and seasonal at Bitter Lake, which is a small thing in July and a real one in January. Neither carries a posted-hours order.

question: Why was this venue missing from other directories?
answer: We can only speak for the commercial dataset we imported, which had no row for it. Seattle Parks does record it. That gap is the reason this project treats a municipal source as the starting point rather than as a cross-check on someone else's list.

question: Is this Magnolia Community Center?
answer: No. The community centre is an indoor building nearby with three courts, recorded separately. We deliberately did not merge them, because merging a playfield with a building is how a directory ends up publishing a court count that belongs to neither.

question: Are there lights?
answer: No. Seattle Parks records no lighting here, and unlike a venue where the city is simply silent, this is a positive record of absence.

question: Is eight courts a lot for Seattle?
answer: It is the joint maximum. Four sites in the city have eight courts and nothing has more: this one, Bitter Lake, Rainier Beach and Green Lake East. Of those four, two are lit and two are not, and West Magnolia is in the unlit half. So this is as much daytime capacity as Seattle offers in one place.

question: Is this the same as Miller Community Center?
answer: No, and they share an address, which is exactly why the distinction matters. The community centre is the indoor building; this is the outdoor playfield with five courts. Our import held both, and treating them as one venue would have doubled the apparent capacity of the block.

question: How many courts are there, really?
answer: Five. The imported record said four. Seattle Parks, which operates the site, records five, and a city record wins on a fact about its own facility.

question: Why is it called Pendleton Miller Playfield on some maps?
answer: That is the name on the city's parcel record. The pickleball dataset calls the same site Miller Playfield, and we use the shorter form the pickleball layer uses.

question: Why does the court count matter so much here?
answer: Because the site is small enough that one court is a large fraction of it. Our imported record said four and the city says five; on an eight-court playfield that would be a rounding error, but on a five-court site it is twenty per cent of the capacity. Venue-name searches are read by people who already know the venue, and they are exactly the readers who would notice.

question: Are there indoor courts at Delridge?
